lead: A directional coupler is a four-port that sends a small, known sample of the wave travelling from port 1 to port 2 to a coupled port, while a wave travelling the other way is sent elsewhere. A meter can then watch the forward and reflected waves without disturbing the line. A hybrid splits power equally: the rat-race gives outputs in phase or 180° apart, the branch-line hybrid 90°. They serve power monitors, reflectometers, balanced mixers and antenna feeds.
prereq: You need: S-matrix tests and dB ratios from S-parameters and the scattering matrix, and guide wavelength λg.

blocks.text: Port 1 is the input, port 2 the through, port 3 the coupled and port 4 the isolated port, all matched. Three positive dB numbers describe the coupler.

C = 10 log₁₀(P₁/P₃) = −20 log₁₀|S₃₁| dB
D = 10 log₁₀(P₃/P₄) = 20 log₁₀(|S₃₁|/|S₄₁|) dB
I = 10 log₁₀(P₁/P₄) = −20 log₁₀|S₄₁| dB = C + D
blocks.where: P₁ is the power fed into port 1 and P₃, P₄ the powers leaving ports 3 and 4. C is the coupling, D the directivity and I the isolation.

blocks.text: A 10 dB coupler sends one tenth of the input to port 3; a 20 dB coupler one hundredth. Directivity says how well the coupler tells forward from reverse; good waveguide couplers reach 30 to 40 dB. The sampled power leaves the main line, so the through port has a coupling loss of −10 log₁₀(1 − 10−C/10) dB: 0.46 dB for a 10 dB coupler.
An ideal coupler is matched, reciprocal and lossless, with the isolated port receiving nothing. Its S-matrix, with |S₂₁| = α, |S₃₁| = β and α² + β² = 1, is
S = [ 0 α jβ 0 ;  α 0 0 jβ ;  jβ 0 0 α ;  0 jβ α 0 ]
blocks.where: rows and columns are ports 1 to 4; the coupled wave leads the through wave by 90°. A wave entering port 2 couples to port 4, so port 4 samples a reflected wave. Check: symmetric, each column sums to α² + β² = 1, and columns are orthogonal.

blocks.text: Two guides share a broad wall with two small holes λg/4 apart. Each hole leaks a little of the main wave into the auxiliary guide, both ways along it.

items: Forward direction (towards port 3): the wave leaking through hole A travels λg/4 in the auxiliary guide to reach hole B; the main wave also travels λg/4 before leaking through B. The two leaked waves have travelled the same distance, so they arrive in phase and add.

Reverse direction (towards port 4): the wave from hole B travels back λg/4 to hole A, while the main wave from hole A did not travel at all. The two paths differ by 2 × λg/4 = λg/2, a 180° difference, so the waves cancel.

blocks.text: The cancellation is exact only where the spacing is λg/4, so directivity falls away from the design frequency; multi-hole couplers with graded hole sizes keep it over a wider band. In WR-90 guide at 10 GHz, λg = 39.8 mm, so the holes are 9.9 mm apart.

A hybrid ring is a closed ring of line with a circumference of 1.5λg and four ports. Going round the ring, number them 1, 2, 3, 4. The arcs are 1–2: λg/4, 2–3: 3λg/4, 3–4: λg/4 and 4–1: λg/4 (total 1.5λg). Each arc is a line of impedance √2 Z₀ (70.7 Ω in a 50 Ω system).
A wave fed into a port runs both ways round the ring. At another port the two parts add when their paths differ by whole wavelengths and cancel when they differ by λg/2.

So port 1 is the sum port: fed there, ports 2 and 4 get half the power each, in phase, and port 3 gets nothing. Port 3 is the difference port: fed there, ports 2 and 4 get half each, 180° apart, and port 1 gets nothing. Ports 1 and 3 are isolated from each other, and so are ports 2 and 4. Signals fed into ports 2 and 4 together give their sum at port 1 and their difference at port 3, like the H- and E-arms of the magic tee in Waveguide tees. The 180° comes from the 3λg/4 arc being λg/2 longer than a λg/4 arc; on its own it is 270° of line.

blocks.where: rows and columns are ports 1 to 4 in the numbering above. Symmetric, matched, and every column has two entries of magnitude 1/√2, so it is unitary.

blocks.text: A branch-line hybrid is a square of four λg/4 lines (two of Z₀ and two of Z₀/√2). It splits equally with a 90° difference between the outputs, so it is called a quadrature hybrid.

examples.question: A directional coupler with 10 dB coupling and 20 dB directivity is fed with 20 dBm at port 1; all other ports are matched. Find the power at the coupled, isolated and through ports in dBm and mW.
steps: Coupled port: P₃ = P₁ − C = 20 − 10 = 10 dBm = 10 mW.
Isolation I = C + D = 10 + 20 = 30 dB, so P₄ = 20 − 30 = −10 dBm = 0.1 mW.
Through port (lossless coupler): P₂ = 100 − 10 − 0.1 = 89.9 mW = 10 log₁₀ 89.9 = 19.54 dBm, a coupling loss of 0.46 dB.
examples.answer: P₃ = 10 dBm (10 mW), P₄ = −10 dBm (0.1 mW), P₂ = 19.54 dBm (89.9 mW).

examples.question: A reflectometer uses a 20 dB coupler with 30 dB directivity to measure a load whose true return loss is 20 dB (|Γ| = 0.1). (a) Find |S₃₁|, |S₄₁| and the through loss of the coupler. (b) With 30 dBm incident, compare the reflected sample with the directivity leak at the same detector, and find the range of |Γ| the instrument may show.
steps: Lossless coupler: |S₂₁| = √(1 − 0.1² − 0.00316²) = 0.995, a through loss of 0.044 dB.
Reflected wave: 30 − 20 = 10 dBm, coupled to the reverse detector at 10 − 20 = −10 dBm. The forward wave leaks there by the isolation: 30 − 50 = −20 dBm, only 10 dB below the wanted sample.
In waves the detector sees 0.1|Γ| plus a leak of 0.1 × 0.0316 (30 dB is a ratio of 0.0316). They may add or subtract, so the reading of |Γ| lies between 0.1 − 0.0316 = 0.068 and 0.1 + 0.0316 = 0.132.
In return loss: between −20 log₁₀ 0.132 = 17.6 dB and −20 log₁₀ 0.068 = 23.3 dB, for a load that is really 20 dB.
examples.answer: |S₃₁| = 0.1, |S₄₁| = 0.0032, through loss 0.044 dB. The 30 dB directivity lets the reading of a 20 dB return-loss load fall anywhere from 17.6 dB to 23.3 dB; measuring well-matched loads needs a directivity well above their return loss.

traps: Mixing up coupling and directivity. Coupling compares port 3 with port 1; directivity compares port 3 with port 4; isolation compares port 1 with port 4, and I = C + D.
Using 10 log with |S| values. |S| is a wave ratio, so C = −20 log₁₀|S₃₁|; with powers use 10 log₁₀(P₁/P₃). Mixing them doubles or halves every answer.
Numbering a rat-race wrongly. The isolated pair is the two ports whose paths differ by λg/2; with the 3λg/4 arc between ports 2 and 3, ports 1 and 3 are isolated and port 1 is the sum port.
Saying the 3λg/4 arc "gives 180°". It is 270° of line; the 180° is its difference from a λg/4 arc.
Assuming port 4 receives zero. Finite directivity leaks power there, which limits how small a reflection a reflectometer can measure.

quiz.q: Define the coupling, directivity and isolation of a directional coupler.
quiz.a: C = 10 log₁₀(P₁/P₃), D = 10 log₁₀(P₃/P₄), I = 10 log₁₀(P₁/P₄) = C + D, all in dB, with input at port 1, coupled port 3 and isolated port 4.

quiz.q: Why does a large directivity matter in a reflectometer?
quiz.a: The reverse detector should see only the reflected wave. Finite directivity lets part of the forward wave leak to it, and the leak adds to or subtracts from the reflected sample, so small reflections are masked. Directivity must be well above the return loss being measured.

quiz.q: A 20 dB coupler with 25 dB directivity is fed with 30 dBm. Find the coupled and isolated powers.
Explain why the holes of a two-hole coupler are λg/4 apart and what happens at another frequency.
quiz.a: Forward-leaked waves travel equal paths and add; reverse-leaked waves differ by 2 × λg/4 = λg/2 and cancel. At another frequency λg changes, the spacing is no longer λg/4, the reverse waves no longer cancel completely and the directivity falls; the coupling changes much less.

quiz.q: State the circumference of a rat-race and its arc lengths.
quiz.a: Circumference 1.5λg: three arcs of λg/4 and one of 3λg/4, each of impedance √2 Z₀.

quiz.q: A rat-race for a 50 Ω system at 3 GHz is made on alumina, where a 70.7 Ω microstrip has εeff = 6.21. Find λg, the ring circumference and its mean radius.
quiz.a: λg = λ₀/√εeff = 100 mm/√6.21 = 40.1 mm. Circumference = 1.5 × 40.1 = 60.2 mm. Mean radius = 60.2/(2π) = 9.58 mm.

quiz.q: In the rat-race above, 10 mW enters the difference port. What leaves each port?
quiz.a: Port 3 is the difference port: ports 2 and 4 get 5 mW each, 180° apart, and port 1 gets nothing, since its two paths differ by λg/2. A matched ring reflects nothing at port 3.

beyond: Modern couplers are mostly printed: coupled-line couplers on boards and Lange couplers for tight coupling on MMICs. Six-port reflectometers measure complex reflection with power detectors alone. Search for "Lange coupler" and "six-port reflectometer".

figure.caption: Port 1 feeds the coupler; port 2 is the through path, port 3 takes the 10 dB coupled sample, and port 4 takes leakage 30 dB below input.

spec.aria: Four-port directional coupler: input at port 1 gives a through wave at port 2, a 10 dB coupled wave at port 3 and a 30 dB isolated wave at port 4.
